subject: technology
essential_question: How can understanding design thinking for real users help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Algorithms and Programming
Michigan Computer Science: Impacts of Computing
project_brief: Design, test, and improve a simple prototype that helps a real or fictional user, with a short presentation. This is the grade 4 culminating project for "Design Thinking for Real Users" (ma-g4-tech-cs-u06, unit 6), built around identifying user needs, requirements and constraints, building a prototype, gathering feedback, and iterating on a design. Design, test, and improve a simple prototype that helps a real or fictional user, with a short presentation. Use only fictional examples, sandbox tools, or already-approved data — never a real account, real credential, or live external system.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: identifying user needs, requirements and constraints, building a prototype, gathering feedback, iterating on a design, and accessibility and inclusion in design.
Meet the performance task as written: Design, test, and improve a simple prototype that helps a real or fictional user, with a short presentation.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Design, test, and improve a simple prototype that helps a real or fictional user, with a short presentation. Use only fictional examples, sandbox tools, or already-approved data — never a real account, real credential, or live external system.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to identifying user needs or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering identifying user needs in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to requirements and constraints, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
